vignette:
The Weight of the Forest

Boon-Nam is a 47-year-old Thai-Australian man who has worked as a park ranger in a national park in Queensland for nearly two decades. He knows the trails the way most people know their own homes - by feel, by smell, by the particular quality of light filtering through the canopy at different hours. He is, by most accounts, a steady and capable man. His colleagues describe him as someone who keeps his head in a crisis. His wife, Malee, would have said the same thing, once.

Three years ago, their nine-year-old son, Kiet, collapsed during a school swimming carnival. What followed was eleven days in a pediatric intensive care unit, a bacterial meningitis diagnosis, and a period during which the doctors spoke to Boon-Nam and Malee in the careful, measured tones people use when they are preparing parents for the possibility that their child will not survive. Kiet did survive. He recovered, largely, though he lost partial hearing in his left ear. Boon-Nam sat beside that hospital bed for eleven days and watched the monitors and listened to the machines and tried to remember how to breathe.

Kiet is twelve now and plays football on weekends. Boon-Nam watches from the sideline and cannot explain to anyone - not to Malee, not to himself - why watching his son run across a green field sometimes makes him feel as though the ground is dissolving beneath his feet. His heart hammers. His vision narrows. He scans the field compulsively for signs that something is wrong, that Kiet is about to fall, that the ordinary afternoon is about to crack open the way it did three years ago.

At work, Boon-Nam moves through the park with the same practiced ease he always has, and this is the place he feels most like himself. But even here, the intrusions find him. He will be checking a trail marker or responding to a visitor's question and without warning he is back in that hospital corridor, fluorescent-lit and airless, watching a doctor's face for information before the words arrive. He has learned to turn away from visitors when this happens, to face the tree line until the feeling passes. He tells himself it is nothing. He has told himself this for three years.

He sleeps badly. He wakes most nights between two and three in the morning, his chest tight, his mind already moving through worst-case scenarios - Kiet choking, Kiet seizing, Kiet unreachable. He gets up and checks on his son. He has done this so many times that Kiet, who is twelve and perceptive, has started leaving his bedroom door ajar. Boon-Nam does not know whether to feel grateful or ashamed.

He and Malee have grown careful with each other in a way they were not before. She has her own grief from those eleven days, but she has moved through it differently - she talks about it, she cried, she eventually returned to something that resembles ordinary life. Boon-Nam has not cried since the night Kiet was discharged. He is not sure he is capable of it anymore. He describes himself as feeling "behind glass" - present in his life, watching it, but unable to quite touch it. He no longer takes much pleasure in the things that once anchored him: the early morning drives into the park, the particular silence of the bush before heat sets in, the cold beer at the end of a long shift.

What he carries, though he would not use this language, is the memory of powerlessness - of sitting beside a small bed and understanding, fully and bodily, that love is not protection. The forest around him is alive and constant and indifferent, and most days he finds something close to comfort in that. But the knowledge he gained in that hospital room has not left him, and he does not yet know what to do with it.
